### Prerequisites

This text continues the study of the Etruscan-Roman numbers. Therefore, we recommend reading the previous texts about their origin (<htcite0>) and about how to write numbers with their seven symbols (<htcite1>) before continuing.

### Introduction

In the texts we have studied so far, we saw three different abacuses, all of them created in Asia: the Soroban, the Suanpan (算盤) and the Schyoty (счёты) (<htcite0>; <htcite1>; <htcite2>). We also learned about the Yupana, a tool to calculate created by the Indigenous peoples of the Andes, in *Abya Yala* (America) (<htcite3>).

Reflection 1: And Europe?

We have seen calculating tools created in Asia, such as the Soroban, the Suanpan (算盤) and the Schyoty (счёты), and in Abya Yala (America), such as the Yupana. Given the knowledge exchanged between peoples, do you believe that Europe also created a tool to calculate?

### Ábaco na Europa

Apesar de estarmos falando do ábacus romano, aparentemente os romanos não foram os primeiros a chegar à conclusão de que esta ferramenta era útil na Europa.

#### Resolvendo uma necessidade
As primeiras evidências do ábaco na Europa são o tablete encontrado na ilha de Salamina, Grécia, datado de <htdate0> (<htcite0>; <htcite1>).

Segundo Keith E. Sugden, os gregos teriam tido necessidade de agilizar seus cálculos enquanto realizavam expansão comercial e negociavam no mar Mediterrâneo, motivo pelo qual criaram ferramentas de cálculo. Além disso, os romanos possuíam uma notação mais simples, que facilitava operações como soma e subtração (<htcite2>).

#### Em Roma

Apesar de utilizarmos o nome "ábaco" para o instrumento romano, não há nenhuma evidência de que eles tenham utilizado esse nome para sua ferramenta de cálculo. O termo mais comum era *calculi* (<htcite3>).

O instrumento que chegou até nós nos lembra muito os ábacos criados na China (Zhongguo, 中國) e no Japão (Nippon koku or Nihon koku, 日本国), ou seja, haveria uma divisão com um marcador superior possuindo o valor 5 (V) e os inferiores possuindo valores unitários (I) (<htcite4>; <htcite5>).

### The Roman abacus

In the reflection, we asked whether Europe also created a tool to calculate. The answer is yes: to calculate, the Romans used their own abacus, which has a shape similar to the Soroban (<htcite0>). Like the Soroban, each of its columns has an upper bead that counts for 5 and four lower beads that each count for 1.

In the application below, we use the columns of the archaeological Roman abacus. From left to right, they are marked (((I))), ((I)), (I), C, X and I, which represent the hundred thousands, the ten thousands, the thousands, the hundreds, the tens and the units. In this abacus, one thousand is marked as (I), ten thousand as ((I)) and one hundred thousand as (((I))).

Represent the number that appears below: move the beads of the columns until the value shown is equal to the requested number. While you move the beads, the application shows the number written with Indo-Arabic numerals and with Roman numerals. Click **Restart** to receive a new number and practice again.
